content:
German federal prosecutors said on Thursday they had arrested two Iraqi nationals suspected of belonging to a terrorist organisation that plotted attacks on Jewish and other targets in Europe, including a synagogue in the western city of Cologne.

The two men, identified only as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J. in line with German privacy rules, were detained in Heidelberg and Cologne respectively, prosecutors said. Officers also carried out raids at 17 locations across the states of Baden-Wuerttemberg, Hesse and North Rhine-Westphalia, in one of the largest counterterrorism operations in Germany this year.

Both suspects were due to appear before a judge on Thursday, who will decide whether they remain in pre-trial detention while the investigation continues.

According to prosecutors, Mostafa Al-R. is acquainted with Mohammad Al-Saadi, a man currently on trial in the United States on terrorism charges. Al-Saadi is alleged to be a key figure in a group called Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyah, known by the acronym HAYI, which prosecutors say emerged after the outbreak of the war in Iran earlier this year.

The group is believed to be behind a series of attacks against American, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe from March 2026 onwards, according to the federal prosecutor's office in Karlsruhe. Prosecutors said Al-Saadi and Mostafa Al-R. founded a separate organisation at the end of 2025 to prepare and carry out further attacks in Germany and elsewhere in Europe, raising funds and recruiting people for that purpose. Ameer J. was a member of that organisation, they said.

The most chilling detail in the arrest warrant concerns two consecutive nights in late March 2026. Prosecutors say that, on the organisation's behalf, unidentified perpetrators travelled to a synagogue in Cologne and to another location in a second European city, presumably carrying explosive devices. For reasons that remain unclear, the attacks were never carried out.

That aborted operation is now at the centre of the investigation. Prosecutors have not said why the attackers turned back, whether they were deterred by security, whether their devices failed, or whether they were acting on orders to wait. The unanswered question matters, because it may determine whether the group was testing German security, gathering intelligence for a later attempt, or simply unable to complete its plan.

The case also sheds new light on a network that German and American investigators have been tracking for months. Al-Saadi's trial in the United States, where he faces terrorism charges, is the other half of the same story: prosecutors on both sides of the Atlantic describe a group that operates across borders, using personal connections and shared ideology to link cells in Europe with figures facing justice in America. The German arrests may provide evidence that prosecutors in the United States can use, and vice versa.

The Cologne synagogue at the centre of the alleged plot is one of Germany's most prominent Jewish institutions. The synagogue on Roonstrasse, rebuilt after the Second World War, stands in a city with one of the country's oldest Jewish communities, and it has long been protected by police. That a plot allegedly targeted it will deepen unease among Jewish communities in Germany, where synagogues and Jewish schools already operate behind barriers and armed guards.

Germany has seen a sharp rise in antisemitic incidents in recent years, and Jewish community leaders have repeatedly warned that threats once expressed online are increasingly taking the form of concrete attack planning. Thursday's arrests will be read in that context, as evidence that the danger is not only rhetorical but organised, funded and directed from abroad.

The timing is also significant. The arrests come as Europe's security services warn of a growing threat from groups linked to Iran, at a moment when tensions between Tehran and the West remain high over the war in the Middle East and the confrontation over Iran's nuclear programme. [The Trump administration is said to be weighing whether to resume major strikes on Iran after the New Year if talks fail](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/trump-inclined-resume-iran-strikes-after-new-year-november-2026), and the United States has already [destroyed Iranian oil tankers and faced missile retaliation](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/us-destroys-five-iranian-tankers-iran-retaliates-jordan-november-2026) in the Gulf. German prosecutors have not said whether the alleged plot was directed from Tehran, but they describe the group as pro-Iranian, and the link to the war in Iran is explicit in their account of how HAYI came into being.

For now, the immediate questions are practical ones: what did the 17 raids uncover, what charges will the two men face, and whether further arrests will follow. Federal prosecutors said the searches were ongoing on Thursday, and they have not ruled out additional suspects. The two men are presumed innocent until proven guilty, and the case against them will be tested in court.

But the broader warning is already clear. A group that prosecutors say has been operating since March, that allegedly sent people with explosives to a synagogue in Cologne, and that was still recruiting and raising money eight months later, was not a lone pair of extremists. It was, on the prosecutors' account, a network, and Thursday's operation was designed to break it before it could strike. [Read the full Reuters report on the arrests](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/german-police-arrest-two-iraqis-over-alleged-cologne-synagogue-bomb-plot-2026-11-26/)
summary: German federal prosecutors said on Thursday they arrested two Iraqi nationals suspected of belonging to a pro-Iranian terrorist organisation that plotted attacks on Jewish targets in Europe, including a synagogue in Cologne.
title: Germany arrests two Iraqis over alleged Cologne synagogue bomb plot linked to pro-Iranian group
